s: D. State sovereign immunity.
The Eleventh Amendment was adopted in 1795 to overturn Chisholm v. Georgia (1793), which had allowed a citizen of South Carolina to sue Georgia.
Its text bars only suits against a state by citizens of another state or a foreign state.
Hans v. Louisiana (1890) held, however, that states also enjoy immunity from suits by their own citizens, because the Amendment confirms a broader background principle of sovereign immunity.
Alden v. Maine (1999) extended that immunity to private federal claims in state courts.
Routes around immunity.
Consent and waiver.
States may consent to suit, but waiver must be unequivocally expressed.
Congressional abrogation.
Congress must use clear statutory language and act under a valid power.
It may abrogate under § 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment (Fitzpatrick v. Bitzer, 1976), subject to congruence and proportionality.
It may not abrogate under Article I powers such as the Commerce Clause (Seminole Tribe v. Florida, 1996).
Bankruptcy is an exception rooted in the plan of the Convention (Central Virginia Community College v. Katz, 2006).
States also consented in the plan of the Convention to suits involving federal eminent domain and war powers (PennEast, 2021; Torres v. Texas DPS, 2022).
Ex parte Young (1908).
A suit against a state officer for prospective injunctive relief to stop an ongoing violation of federal law is not a suit against the state.
Retrospective monetary relief payable from the state treasury is barred (Edelman v. Jordan, 1974).
Suits by the United States or by other states are not barred.
Local governments (counties, cities) have no Eleventh Amendment immunity, though § 1983 liability requires an official policy or custom (Monell).
Individual officers sued for damages in their personal capacity may raise qualified immunity, a separate doctrine.
Is a suit against a state barred?
Is the defendant the state or an arm of the state, rather than a municipality or an officer sued personally?
Did the state unequivocally waive immunity?
Did Congress clearly abrogate immunity under a valid power (Fourteenth Amendment § 5; bankruptcy)?
Is this an Ex parte Young suit for prospective relief against an officer?
Is the plaintiff the United States or another state?
